card.hook: Stand at the foot of the ridge and crane your neck: walls, towers and rooflines pile up above you like a stone wedding cake. Even a quick snap looks dramatic here.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map on Obere Schmiedgasse, and face north-east. You'll be shooting up at the walls, not across at them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole mass of stone, then switch to 1x for a more natural view. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for tower tops and roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up a tower or wall edge with a vertical line so the buildings don't lean, then tap the brightest stonework and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the sandstone more than harsh midday sun. Earlier in the day is often quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Head to the city-wall walkway above the Tiergärtnertor (Animal Gardener's Gate), reached through the southern castle garden. Use the front camera and frame the shot so the castle rises behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Tiergärtnertor Platz, a square directly below the castle, where the whole Kaiserburg is in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the castle may need tickets and have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole ridge, then hunt down three details: a tower top, a gateway and a timber-framed corner.
card.good_to_know: The first fortified buildings appear to date from around 1000, and German kings and emperors stayed here for centuries. Look for the round Sinwell Tower, a keep from the later 13th century that gained an extra floor in the 1560s. Much of the castle was ruined in the air raids of 1944/45 and rebuilding took about thirty years, so what you see is a careful restoration.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map on Obere Schmiedgasse, and face north-east. You'll be shooting up at the walls, not across at them.

selfie_spots.detail: On the defensive passage of the city wall, above the Tiergärtnertor gate, reached from the southern castle garden (Burggarten). Frame the shot so the castle rises behind you.
selfie_spots.why: One guide calls this the most beautiful view of Old Nuremberg, and from it the Kaiserburg is visible above the rooftops, so it can serve as a backdrop.

card.hook: A sharp glass-and-steel wedge cuts straight through a huge, heavy stone hall, and your eye goes right to it. It's a serious place, so take your photos calmly and quietly.
card.stand_here: Stand about 65 m north-west of the Documentation Center and face south-east, looking straight at it. The glass wedge and the stone hall will sit together in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the wedge and the hall around it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the glass against the stone. Use 0.5x only if you're close and want to show how big the building is, and keep the horizon level.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the glass wedge off-centre, then tap the building and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a still day if you're trying the lake shore, because the water may give you a reflection of the hall. Keep the water in the bottom third of your photo.
card.selfie_here: A Tripadvisor reviewer recommends standing by the lake for a dramatic angle on the building, so try the Großer Dutzendteich side of the rally grounds. Use the front camera (0.5x if you need more of the building in), keep the building over your shoulder, and keep it simple and respectful rather than a big pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the wide parade road behind the lake, with you at the water's edge and the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed outdoors, but restrictions apply indoors, and drones and commercial photography need permission. Please avoid insensitive photos, especially selfies at memorials, and stay out of other visitors' way.
card.challenge: Find the exact spot where the glass meets the curved stone, and get that line on one of your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The Documentation Center sits inside the north wing of the Congress Hall, which was planned for 50,000 people but never finished. Austrian architect Günther Domenig won the 1998 competition with the glass-and-steel passageway, and it was unveiled on 4 November 2001. The museum has been rebuilding and running an interim exhibition, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 65 m north-west of the Documentation Center and face south-east, looking straight at it. The glass wedge and the stone hall will sit together in one frame.

card.hook: This one isn't pretty, and that's why it's worth a photo: a big, formal courthouse with a serious story behind every stone. You're not here for a sunset, you're here to remember what you saw.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Palace of Justice, right where the phone icon sits on the map, so there's no extra walk. Face the building and take a few steps back to fit more of the facade in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the whole building from close range, then go to 1x for a more natural look. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for doorways, signs and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so it doesn't lean back when you tilt the phone up.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day is kind to big stone buildings, because the light is soft and even. If it's sunny, check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive and wait until it reaches the front.
card.selfie_here: Try the street corner where Benjamin-Ferencz-Platz meets Fürther Straße, in front of the Palace of Justice. It's a spot where the building has been photographed well, though it isn't a proven selfie spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the courthouse over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside a museum can change from room to room, and Courtroom 600 is a historic space, so ask staff or check the official site before you go. Be respectful of other visitors and avoid shots that put strangers in the foreground.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one straight-edged wide picture of the whole building, then one close-up of a doorway or sign that tells the story on its own.
card.good_to_know: The Nuremberg Trials were held in this courthouse between 1945 and 1949. The museum's permanent exhibition opened on 21 November 2010 in the attic of the east wing, directly above Courtroom 600. Since March 2020 that courtroom is no longer used for court hearings and is part of the museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Palace of Justice, right where the phone icon sits on the map, so there's no extra walk. Face the building and take a few steps back to fit more of the facade in.

selfie_spots.why: A photographer's shot of the building was taken from this corner, so it is a documented vantage point for framing the palace, though no page calls it a selfie spot.

card.hook: Picture 27 tall white concrete columns marching in a line towards a glass-and-sandstone museum, with open sky behind them. On this street, the street is the star and the museum is the backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand on Straße der Menschenrechte at the north end, by the information panel that lists the 27 columns, and face south. The columns lead your eye straight to the museum front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole row and the museum front in one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x (if your phone has it) to bring the museum closer and squeeze the columns together.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, line yourself up with the row so the columns march away evenly, and tap the columns; if the sky looks washed out, drag the brightness slider down a little.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is likely to be calmer, so fewer people will wander between you and the columns. It's an open-air street, so you can take your time.
card.selfie_here: Step in among the white columns near the museum's main entrance on Kartäusergasse and use the front camera at 0.5x. Let the columns fill the frame behind you, with the sky above.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement along Kartäusergasse and shoot the row wide at 0.5x, while you stand among the columns so the whole walkway fits in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography at the Way of Human Rights is permitted. Inside the museum, flash is not allowed and some special exhibitions restrict photos, so check the signs at each hall entrance.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the columns are perfectly straight and evenly spaced, then one where you're the only thing out of line.
card.good_to_know: The Germanisches Nationalmuseum, founded in 1852, is Germany's largest museum of cultural history. It grew from the remains of a medieval charterhouse. The glass entrance hall on this street is part of the 1988 to 1993 extension by Jan Störmer, and the Israeli sculptor Dani Karavan turned Kartäusergasse into the Way of Human Rights.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Straße der Menschenrechte at the north end, by the information panel that lists the 27 columns, and face south. The columns lead your eye straight to the museum front.

card.hook: Picture a 19-metre stone spire poking up over the market stalls like it's trying to win a game of hide and seek, and failing. That's the Beautiful Fountain, and it's very hard to miss.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Hauptmarkt and stand about 15 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. If the top of the spire gets cut off, take a few steps back.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole spire and the square in one shot, or try zoom 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the carved details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter on the square, so you get a cleaner shot. A bright, slightly overcast day also gives soft light that shows the stonework evenly.
card.selfie_here: Guides say visitors lean on the iron railing on the fountain's south-west side to have their photos taken. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and check that the spire is over your shoulder before you smile, because the framing is worth checking on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Hauptmarkt opposite the Frauenkirche, where the fountain is in view across the square, while you pose over by the fountain.
card.rules_and_safety: If the market is on, stalls may block your view, and for special events check the official site before you go. One guide advises avoiding the area south of the train station at night.
card.challenge: Get the spire dead straight on a grid line with a little sky above its tip. No leaning allowed!
card.good_to_know: Heinrich Beheim built the fountain between 1385 and 1396, and it's one of the main attractions on Nuremberg's Historical Mile. It's shaped like a Gothic spire. During World War II it was surrounded by concrete to protect it from bombing, which is a nice fact to share with friends along with your picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Hauptmarkt and stand about 15 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. If the top of the spire gets cut off, take a few steps back.

card.hook: St. Lorenz has two tall towers, a sharply pointed doorway and a rose window 9 metres across, so the big question is how much of it you squeeze in. Start with all of it, then go hunting for details.
card.stand_here: Stand near Lorenzer Platz, about 10 m west of the church, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and you're looking straight at the west front with both towers, the portal and the rose window.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and the doorway in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the rose window and the carved doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep your phone upright and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Try the afternoon or early evening, when sunlight is likely to fall on the west front. At dusk, night mode can capture the lit facade, but brace your arms against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the bronze Tugendbrunnen (Virtue Fountain) on Lorenzer Platz and stand by it with the Gothic facade behind you. Use the front camera and, if your phone offers 0.5x there, switch to it so more of the church fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street or out on Lorenzer Platz, so the whole facade and both towers fit in the frame with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the church. It's a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and any rules about photography or dress.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the whole front, then one of just the rose window, and see if you can catch a passer-by walking through the first one to show how big the church is.
card.good_to_know: St. Lorenz is a medieval church in Nuremberg, once a free imperial city. The nave was finished around 1400, and the hall-style choir was largely complete by 1477. Inside are a carving of the Angelic Salutation by Veit Stoss and a monumental tabernacle by Adam Kraft, which includes a figure of the sculptor himself.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Lorenzer Platz, about 10 m west of the church, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and you're looking straight at the west front with both towers, the portal and the rose window.

card.hook: St. Sebaldus has twin towers so tall you'll want to tilt your head back, and your phone will happily lean right along with you. Keep it level and you get the proper postcard: dark sandstone filling the frame, with the Old Town Hall tucked in beside it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Albrecht-Dürer-Platz, in front of the church, and face the west façade. Keep the Old Town Hall at one edge of the frame so the two buildings sit together.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic church-plus-town-hall view. If the towers won't fit from the square, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for stonework and sculpture details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the church's vertical edges up with them, then tap the stonework and slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright so the sandstone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the stone. Early in the day the square is also likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Albrecht-Dürer-Platz with the church front behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the towers in over your shoulder, and hold the phone level. For a different angle, try Irrerstraße, where the towers come into view if you find the right spot, but check the framing when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pavement opposite the church, in front of the rectory with the sandstone oriel, while you stand with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The exterior is photographed from the open public square. Inside, photos are generally fine but without flash, and with respect for worship and events. One sculpture, the antisemitic Judensau relief from the 1380s, is about 7 m up on the exterior. You can leave it out of your frame or include it deliberately.
card.challenge: Get both towers dead straight against your gridlines, with the Old Town Hall in the frame and not a single leaning wall.
card.good_to_know: The church is named after Sebaldus, an 8th-century hermit and missionary who is Nuremberg's patron saint. Building began in 1225, and by about 1273–75 it was a Romanesque basilica with two choirs. The late Gothic hall chancel and taller steeples came in the 14th and 15th centuries, and it was restored after heavy damage in the Second World War.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Albrecht-Dürer-Platz, in front of the church, and face the west façade. Keep the Old Town Hall at one edge of the frame so the two buildings sit together.

card.hook: Here's a fun twist: the best photo of the Henkersteg isn't taken on the Henkersteg. Photo guides say to stand on the Maxbrücke instead, where the covered bridge, the round Henkerturm and the half-timbered Weinstadel line up on the river like a postcard.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the Maxbrücke in Nuremberg's Old Town and face upstream along the river. The Henkersteg is to the south from here.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which holds the bridge, tower and Weinstadel together. Tap 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the covered bridge and the tower. Save zoom 0.5x for Unschlittplatz, and keep the buildings away from the edges of the frame there.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water on the lower third, and hold your phone low just above the parapet so the reflection fills more of the picture.
card.best_time: Pick a calm day, because still water can give a near-mirror reflection that doubles the picture. Check how the light falls on the buildings when you arrive, and if the sky is bright, drag the brighter/darker slider down a touch so the timber keeps its detail.
card.selfie_here: Try the Unschlittplatz riverbank at the south end of the bridge, where the covered bridge meets the Henkerturm and the square. It's an often-photographed backdrop spot. Use the front camera and put the bridge over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Maxbrücke to shoot upstream toward the Henkersteg while you stand on the bridge's walkway in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stop in the middle of the Maxbrücke but step to the side, so you don't block people walking past.
card.challenge: Take three frames: bridge on the left with the tower on the right, then the reverse, then one wide shot of the whole scene. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Henkersteg is a covered wooden footbridge over the Pegnitz in Nuremberg's Old Town. The round Henkerturm stands right beside it, and the half-timbered Weinstadel with its water tower sits on the river next to them. Together they make a compact, old-fashioned scene that suits a phone screen well.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the Maxbrücke in Nuremberg's Old Town and face upstream along the river. The Henkersteg is to the south from here.

The visitor-on-the-walkway part of the passer-by setup is also inferred: the sources recommend the Maxbrücke for photos of the whole bridge but do not say who should stand where. The sources say the bridge is best photographed from the Maxbrücke, and one says the Maxbrücke is downstream of the bridge. No page gave selfie-stick or tripod rules, and no safety point was stated. One review mentions bird droppings, which I left out as hygiene rather than safety. The provided coordinates (49.45311, 11.07306) were not checked against any page.

card.hook: Turn up around midday and the church puts on a show: a bell rings, trumpeters and a drummer appear, and the electors march around the Emperor. The busy west front is why it photographs so well, so ignore the plain sides.
card.stand_here: Stand near Plobenhofstraße, about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there you get the front and the gable together without leaning your phone back.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole west front. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the gable, the clock and the porch sculptures. Use 0.5x only if crowds or stalls push you much closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the stone, then drag the brightness down a touch so the sky and pale front keep their detail.
card.best_time: Around midday, when the Männleinlaufen clock performs. Try a Live Photo to catch the figures moving. Afternoon or evening may give the west front nicer light, but expect crowds at midday.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone slightly above eye level. Keep the landmark over your shoulder and tilt the phone until the building behind you looks straight.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the Hauptmarkt, where the whole church fits in the frame, while you stand closer to the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is on a public square. If you go inside, be quiet and respectful, and check the official site first for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Can you keep the central tower on the middle gridline and the phone dead level, with the Emperor's parade still in the shot?
card.good_to_know: Emperor Charles IV had the church built between 1352 and 1362. The gable you see today dates from 1506 to 1508 and was designed by Adam Kraft. The church was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War, and repairs were finished by 1953.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Plobenhofstraße, about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there you get the front and the gable together without leaning your phone back.

ask_someone_spot.name: Hauptmarkt (Main Market Square), centre of the square
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand in the middle of the square so the whole Frauenkirche fits in the frame, with the church at the eastern end of the Hauptmarkt. Use a wide-angle setting if you can. The Frauenkirche is at Hauptmarkt 14.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor stands with the Frauenkirche directly behind them, so selfie_spots is empty rather than guessed. The Hauptmarkt is named as the place to photograph the church from, and the Schöner Brunnen (fountain) is named as a separate landmark in the same square, but neither page describes a selfie position with the church behind. The ask-someone spot is the centre of the Hauptmarkt, which the Locationscout page gives as the place to include the entire church; it describes that position for a photographer, not a visitor pose. No page I found mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, or a safety point, for this site.

card.hook: There's a brightly painted rooster rider perched on a pipe in front of a very old house, and he looks like he hopped out of a wooden toy box. That's the Gockelreiterbrunnen (Rooster Rider Fountain), and he's your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the fountain at the front of the Nuremberg Toy Museum, Karlstraße 13–15. Get close to the rooster and face the house, so the old façade rises behind him.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the rooster and the lower part of the house. If the whole façade won't fit, tap 0.5x. Try zoom 2x or 5x for the oriel up high (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the rooster, then slide the brightness down a little so his colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in daytime, when the rooster's colours look best. Overcast light is fine too, and it avoids harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Karlstraße pavement in front of the museum (Karlstraße 13–15), facing the house with the gable behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold it a bit low so the gable fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain is outside at the museum's front. Check the museum's official site for opening and entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Put the rooster in the bottom third of the frame, then take a second shot from further back to see how much of the house you can squeeze in behind him.
card.good_to_know: The house goes back to 1517. Its street side was rebuilt in 1611 and the oriel (a chörlein) followed around 1720. The house was badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt, and the museum opened here in 1971. Michael Mathias Prechtl designed the fountain for that opening, and the collection inside, around 87,000 objects, grew from the private collection of Lydia and Paul Bayer, which the city took over in 1966.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the fountain at the front of the Nuremberg Toy Museum, Karlstraße 13–15. Get close to the rooster and face the house, so the old façade rises behind him.

selfie_spots.name: Karlstraße, in front of the museum's Renaissance gable facade (Karlstraße 13–15)
selfie_spots.detail: on the Karlstraße pavement facing the house, with the gable behind you
selfie_spots.why: The former townhouse has a richly decorated gable on a plain building body, and the museum's facade is the feature pages photograph most, so it makes the strongest backdrop.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence: no page I found names a specific standing spot for a selfie or a passer-by photo of the visitor with the whole facade. The Karlstraße spot is my inference from pages that show the facade and give the street address, not a named photo spot. Wanderlog and Belinda Shi list the Toy Museum among photo spots but give no location detail. Pages on the Hauptmarkt, Kaiserburg and Weißgerbergasse mention good photo motifs, but none ties them to the museum. One page says photography is generally allowed inside for personal, non-commercial use, and that signed exceptions apply (wonderfulmuseums.com). No page I found mentions selfie sticks or tripods, so no rule is given. Please verify the Karlstraße spot on site, for example whether the pavement is wide enough for a clear backdrop.

card.hook: It's called the Meat Bridge, which sounds a bit unglamorous, but look at it: one very flat stone arch, curving calmly over the Pegnitz with old town buildings all around. It's a lovely, simple shape to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near Findelgasse, about 160 m east of the bridge. Face west and you'll have the bridge ahead of you, though buildings or trees may block part of the view.
card.zoom: From the phone icon, start at zoom 1x to get the bridge in its setting. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to bring the arch closer. Once you're right next to the bridge, use 0.5x along the parapet to show how wide it is, and 2x for a close-up of the portal.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the arch up with the horizontal lines so that flat curve looks nice and even, with a bit of river along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters stonework. The shaded old town streets can be dim, so check the light on the day.
card.selfie_here: Go to the Ochsenportal at the bridge's end, by the reclining bronze ox. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you're close, and keep the bridge arch behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the Museumsbrücke and ask them to face the Fleischbrücke, so the whole bridge is in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally unrestricted here, but commercial photography or drones may need permits. Check the official site before you go in case of events or works.
card.challenge: Find the Latin inscription on the portal, get a close-up of it, and then try to spot the ox that was never a calf.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was built between 1596 and 1598 to replace an earlier stone-and-wood bridge that floods kept destroying. At 15.3 m wide with a 27 m clear span, it was the largest masonry bridge arch in Germany when it was finished. The arch rises only 4.2 m, which is why it looks so flat, and the bridge came through the Second World War almost unscathed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon near Findelgasse, about 160 m east of the bridge. Face west and you'll have the bridge ahead of you, though buildings or trees may block part of the view.

selfie_spots.why: The ox is the bridge's best-known photo feature, and one guide says it provides a unique photo opportunity, though no page describes a selfie framing.

selfie_research.notes: Coordinates 49°27'10.4"N 11°4'36.5"E (Wikidata) match the given position. No page clearly describes a selfie with the bridge behind the visitor; the selfie spots are inferred from ox-portal and bridge-view pages. Sources conflict on the ox's location: one says 'center of the bridge', while others place the Ochsenportal at the bridge's end on Hauptmarkt 1. card.hook: Most people shoot Dürer's house from the square, craning their necks at the steep roof. Go up and look down on it instead, and you'll get the picture nobody else in the crowd has.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Sinwellturm, on the city wall walkway near the Tiergärtnertor, and face the house so you're looking down on its roof and half-timbered front. Check on site that the walkway is open before you climb up.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the roof and facade. Then drop to 1x to bring in the neighbouring rooftops. If you end up at street level, zoom 0.5x helps in the narrow street or the square.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the bright sandstone and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the dark timbers and pale stone than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the small square in front of the house (Tiergärtnertorplatz) and stand beside the bronze Dürer statue. Use the front camera, hold it a bit wide (0.5x if your phone offers it) and keep the house over your shoulder, with the castle rising behind it.
card.ask_someone: If the wall walkway is open, ask a passer-by to stand up there looking down, while you stand in the square, so the whole house and the castle behind fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed inside the house, and some areas or temporary exhibitions may restrict photos, so follow the posted signs. The old wooden stairs inside are worn smooth and can be slippery, so wear shoes with good grip.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the roof ridge up with one, and keep the timber lines dead straight. No leaning house allowed!
card.good_to_know: Albrecht Dürer lived here from 1509 until his death in 1528, and the five-storey house dates from around 1420. It has been a museum about him since 1871. Bombing badly damaged it in October 1944, and it was rebuilt by 1949 and reopened as a museum in 1971.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Sinwellturm, on the city wall walkway near the Tiergärtnertor, and face the house so you're looking down on its roof and half-timbered front. Check on site that the walkway is open before you climb up.

selfie_spots.name: Dürer monument in the square in front of the house (Tiergärtnertorplatz)
selfie_spots.detail: beside the bronze Dürer statue on the small square in front of the house, with the house behind you and the castle rising behind it
selfie_spots.why: The bronze monument, the timber-framed house and the castle on the hill form a layered backdrop that works for a close-up selfie.

selfie_research.safety: The original wooden staircases inside the house have been worn smooth over centuries and can be slippery, so wear shoes with good grip.
selfie_research.notes: No page names a spot specifically for taking selfies with the house behind; the selfie spot is inferred from photo guides describing the square and monument in front of the house. Sources disagree on the monument's location: Adventure Lion puts it on Albrecht-Dürer-Platz, while Chasing Hippoz and Quartiere place it in the square in front of the house (Tiergärtnertorplatz). The ask-someone spot is a photographer's vantage point from the Flickr photo caption and Quartiere's description of the wall walkway; no page recommends it for photographing visitors, so verify the walkway is open to the public. Chasing Hippoz's tip about standing at the far end of the square is for shooting the monument with the house behind, not a selfie. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Most of the old town is gabled houses and church spires, then this stout red tower turns up on a corner like it took a wrong turn in the 13th century. Around 1430 Nuremberg is said to have had about 65 of them, and this is the last one.
card.stand_here: Walk to the spot near Lorenzer Platz, about 65 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face west and the whole tower is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole tower in. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the coat of arms frieze and the little pointed turrets. Only use 0.5x if you have to stand very close, and expect the walls to lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line a vertical edge of the corner up with one so the walls stay straight, then tap the sunlit stone and slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go on an overcast day or later in the afternoon. The soft light shows off the texture of the sandstone and keeps harsh shadows off the frieze.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the cobbled Lorenzer Platz plaza in front of the tower's facade, with the tower behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and let the corner turrets peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza side across Königstraße, facing the tower, so the whole tower and its roofline fit in the frame while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the street. The cellar is an inn and the tower is owned by a foundation, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
card.challenge: Spot the three little corner turrets, then try to work out which one is the original. Hint: only the left-hand one survived.
card.good_to_know: The cellar and two lower floors date from the 13th century, and the two upper floors were added in the 15th. The tower was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt between 1950 and 1954, so much of the frieze is renewed. The name 'Nassau House' has only been used since the 19th century and rests on a mistaken link to a medieval German king.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the spot near Lorenzer Platz, about 65 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face west and the whole tower is in front of you.

selfie_spots.name: Lorenzer Platz plaza, in front of the tower
selfie_spots.detail: on the cobbled pedestrian plaza in front of the tower's facade, with the tower behind you
selfie_spots.why: Reviewers single out the open plaza around the tower as a good picture setting, and the tower's facade with its corner turrets and bay window is the main thing to frame.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by the pages I found; no page gives a precise standing point for either the selfie or the passer-by photo, so both 'detail' entries are my inference from the tower's position across Königstraße from St. Lorenz Church and on the Lorenzer Platz plaza. A Quartiere page describes a 1900-era view with the Tugendbrunnen standing in front of the tower on Lorenzer Platz; I could not confirm a fountain there today, so do not use it as a landmark. The tower is also described as being at Königstraße and Karolinenstraße (corner, Karolinenstr. 2). No rules on selfie sticks or tripods and no safety point were stated on any page I found.

card.hook: Look up along the roofline: little 'dwarf houses' stand up there like tiny neighbours peeking over the edge. Nuremberg's Town Hall is long, calm and a bit showy, and those three Baroque portals break up the windows nicely.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Hauptmarkt, where the Schöner Brunnen fountain stands beside the Town Hall and the Frauenkirche is close by. Face the Town Hall and keep the fountain low in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the fountain and Town Hall together. Try 0.5x if you want the fountain big in the foreground, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the portals and roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the long roofline with a horizontal line, then tap the brightest part of the facade and slide it a little darker so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Expect other visitors in the square whenever you go, so be patient and take a few shots. One of them will have a clear gap.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the Rathausplatz, on the square in front of the Town Hall (it's named as its own stop in a Hauptmarkt guide). Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the Town Hall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand beside the Schöner Brunnen on the Hauptmarkt and ask the passer-by to step back across the square so the whole Town Hall fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is generally permitted in public spaces in Nuremberg, but rules can differ inside churches and museums. Getting inside the Town Hall, or on tours and cellars, may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Find the gap where the angled New Town Hall lets you see through to the southern tower of the old building, and frame it as a detail shot.
card.good_to_know: The main building went up between 1616 and 1622 to designs by Jakob Wolff the Younger. Its oldest part, the great hall on the south side, dates from 1332-1340. The complex burned down to its outer walls in 1944-45, and the Old Town Hall was rebuilt between 1956 and 1962.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Hauptmarkt, where the Schöner Brunnen fountain stands beside the Town Hall and the Frauenkirche is close by. Face the Town Hall and keep the fountain low in front of you.
